newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION - "EURO-PHOBIA OR EURO-PHORIA?" - BY J. KAYSER.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - "EURO-PHOBIA OR EURO-PHORIA?" - BY J. KAYSER.

text.p: By Jutta Kayser, analyst at Dresdner Bank AG, Frankfurt
Will we never see high interest rates again?

The improving European economy is likely to lead to an increase in yields in 1997. This increase should, however, only be moderate as we already expect a waning economic dynamism in Europe in 1998, with no capacity bottlenecks or wage pressures and low inflation.

According to our medium-term forecast published mid February, interest rates will not move notably higher prior to monetary union and following its introduction than they would be without monetary union. On the one hand it is true that a risk premium will develop until the European central bank has gained the confidence of investors. On the other hand however the financial markets will reward the saving efforts of the budget politicians.

Within the monetary union, where the exchange rate risk disappears, interest rates in individual countries only differ from each other due to the liquidity of the markets, the tax regulations, hedging facilities on the futures markets and the credit standing of issuers.
FAVOURABLE CONDITIONS FOR THE EQUITY MARKETS

In the Dresdner Bank basis-scenario of a core monetary union (with Germany, France, Austria, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland and possibly Finland as participants) the equity markets of the European Union will have a tailwind in the next few years: low interest rates, high exchange rate stability, moderate wage pressure and perceptible improvements in productivity - to name just a few factors.
The economic situation expected by us - moderate growth accompanied by relatively stable prices - provides favourable overall economic conditions for rising share prices.

If we assume increased expansion in production between 1999 and 2001, stagnant or even sinking unit labour costs will perceptibly increase companies' profitability. In addition companies operating within the EU will have no exchange rate hedging costs.

Even more important than the direct cost effects of monetary union on companies' profits are the indirect cost effects. Without monetary union the pressure for reform in the free market economy and also in the public sector would be smaller. In Germany, relaxed shop opening hours, the restriction in dismissal protection and the shortening of the authorization process for investments are just a few examples.

The fundamental reasons for share price developments will gain more importance when exchange rate movements disappear. The country borders are smudged for investors and instead the choice of sectors comes to the fore.

The equity markets in the European Union can be certain of attention over the coming few years. This is especially true of the euro-markets - if only because of their size. The stock market denominated in euros should be more liquid and more transparent than the individual markets and according to estimates will have a capitalisation of 1,100 billion euros (around 1,300 billion US dollars).

Investors who up until now have not included the small European equity markets in their portfolios will no longer be able to ignore the third largest market in the world, a market which after all has a quarter of the US market volume."

Jutta Kayser is analyst in the Macro-Research department of Dresdner Bank AG. The author accepts sole responsibility for the contents of this article. Translation from German into English was carried out by Reuters
